newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban may force Dostum, Masood to bury hatred.
newsitem.headline: Taleban may force Dostum, Masood to bury hatred.

text.p: Afghanistan's former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood and northern militia commander General Abdul Rashid Dostum may have to bury an old rivalry to confront the Islamic Taleban, military experts said on Tuesday.

Militant Taleban warriors, flushed with their capture of Kabul on Friday, have chased Masood's retreating forces, seizing his stronghold of Jabal os-Siraj, 70 km (45 miles) north of the capital, on Monday and pushing 10 km (six miles) east on Tuesday to Golbahar at the foot of the rugged Panjsher Valley.

Taleban forces also thrust north of Jabal os-Siraj until they came up against Dostum's troops, who had taken up defensive positions several kilometres (miles) south of the strategic Soviet-built Salang Tunnel.

The two-year-old Islamic militia's sweeping gains have given it control of about three-quarters of Afghanistan's 33 provinces, but foreign military experts said it was too early to write off Dostum and Masood.

"The Taleban's capture of Kabul may have been brilliant, but Masood's achievement in managing an orderly retreat with most of his tanks and heavy weapons was just as impressive," said one former Western army officer, who asked not to be named.

Masood has now withdrawn to his Panjsher heartland, whose fearsome terrain he exploited to chew up Soviet forces that tried in vain to secure the valley during their decade-long occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s.
"Masood has undoubted qualities as a strategist and has in the past commanded great loyalty from his men," the Western expert said.

However, the ease with which the Taleban sliced through government defences between the eastern city of Jalalabad and Kabul has raised doubts about whether that loyalty has been eroded during years of factional fighting since mujahideen guerrillas toppled the communist regime in April 1992.

Afghan analysts said the former government's reconciliation with its one-time foe Gulbuddin Hekmatyar earlier this year had dismayed many of Masood's hard-core Tajik followers who had fought Hekmatyar's mainly ethnic Pashtun Hezb-i-Islami faction for so long.

Hekmatyar, who rejoined the government of deposed president Burhanuddin Rabbani as prime minister in June, swiftly lost all his territory to the mainly Pashtun Taleban, who used threat or inducements to persuade many Hezb-i-Islami commanders to switch sides or not to fight.

Masood may have a tough time keeping his forces supplied with food and fuel, especially when winter snows close the 3,848-mere (12,625 feet) high Khawak Pass at the northeastern end of Panjsher in about six weeks' time.
"Much will depend on whether he and Dostum can put their enmity aside and cooperate against the Taleban," a military source said.

Dostum, then defence minister in Rabbani's government, joined Hekmatyar in an attempt to seize Kabul in a military coup on January 1, 1994, setting off a bloody round of fighting with Masood's forces.

He had resisted increasingly urgent overtures from Rabbani for an alliance against the Taleban in recent months, preferring to sit on the fence and avoid antagonising the Islamic radicals as they battled his enemies.

Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, leader of the Taleban's interim shura, or council, in Kabul, said last week he hoped for cooperation with Dostum, who had "shown himself to be a good Moslem" -- a sharp change of tone from the Taleban's previous hostility to Dostum as a former communist.

Dostum, a secular-minded military man, controls six mainly Uzbek northern provinces with well-equipped troops and air force. He is widely believed to receive support from neighbouring Uzbekistan, which, like Russia, fears that the Taleban's Islamic zeal might spill into Central Asian countries.
The Taleban are likely to try the same tactics in Dostum's territory as they have used to great effect elsewhere, attempting to subvert local commanders and to win over tribes and religious leaders.

The Taleban, taught a strict brand of Islam at religious schools for Afghan refugees in Pakistan, have gained the support of many traders who are delighted at the movement's determination to open roads and eliminate guerrilla checkpoints extorting tolls and bribes.

Military experts give some credence to accusations by the previous Rabbani government that the Islamic revolutionaries have received help from Pakistan. Islamabad has frequently denied favouring any Afghan faction.

"Recently the Taleban seem to have acquired new strategic skills and effective command and control systems, as well as the ability to move food, fuel and ammunition forward rapidly to exploit their advances," one expert said.

Afghan and Pakistani witnesses say they have detected the presence of Pakistanis in Taleban ranks, but it is not clear whether these are Islamic soldiers of fortune or have any connection with the Pakistani military.
